en: The Illustrated Chart of the Six Requisites for Bhikṣus as Ordained by the Buddha,
produced in the first month of summer in the third year of the Yuanfeng era of the Great Song by the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Tiantáng Monastery in Yúháng.

1–3. The Three Robes (Tricīvara). 1. Explaining that the three robes constitute three distinct items. First, it is explained that these three robes consist of three separate objects. These robes are of nine grades; here, the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) is shown as the upper grade, while the others are determined by reduction accordingly: the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) has seven strips, and the *antarvāsaka* (inner robe) has five strips. This is observed for those who delight in training in the precepts.
I wish to prepare my dharma robes,
but I do not know how they should be cut;
moreover, I am ignorant of the vinaya rules.
Although one frequently encounters false practices,
the regulations for [proper conduct] are found throughout various texts.
Therefore, I have extracted its essential points and combined what I have seen and heard,
returning to the fundamental principles of the ancient texts.
Furthermore, I shall divide this into ten sections and cite the authentic teachings,
so that there may be a standard for practice to rely upon.
This refers to the prohibition against indiscriminate [accusations];
that is to say, not looking to another's countenance—
this was the original intent of the regulation.
The Commentary states:
What is meant by "regulations"?
It refers to the three robes and six requisites.
The Buddha established the rule that they be kept;
this applies universally to all those who have been transformed by his teaching,
and he likewise prescribed their use and wearing.
To violate this constitutes an offense.
The Sarvāstivādins say:
it is intended to manifest a previously unheard-of phenomenon.
Therefore, among all ninety-six paths, none possess these three names, in order to distinguish them from non-Buddhist paths.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time..."
They all wear robes such as these.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"The three robes are the insignia of the noble śramaṇas. The *Saṃyukta-āgama* states: [as above].
To cultivate the four immeasurables and wear the three dharma robes—
this is the attire of one who possesses compassion.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Because it has been cut with a knife,
one knows this to be the robe of a person possessed of shame and modesty."
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"Those who wear the kāṣāya robe abandon the three poisons."
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"One who harbors the fetters and afflictions should not don the kāṣāya."
The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish says:
"Those who wear the kashaya robe should [strive] within birth and death."
One will swiftly attain liberation.
The *Zhangfu yi* states:
"To summarize its essential conclusion:"
Is it not that these three are the vessel for crossing the sea of suffering and the ladder for leveling the rungs of one's life? Therefore,
all three are required.
The *Fenbie gongde lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merits) states:
"For the sake of the three seasons,
one wears heavy [garments] during winter."
In summer one wears light [garments],
and in spring one wears those of medium weight.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Because the disciples of the Buddha abide in the Middle Way, they wear the three robes (*tricīvara*).

Because the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are naked and shameless, abiding in the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), they go without clothing. Because those in white robes (*avadātavasana*) have much greed and are heavily attached, abiding in the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), [they wear many garments]. As the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
A single robe cannot ward off the cold,
whereas the three robes can.
The *Jie tan jing* (Sīmāmaṇḍala Sūtra) says:
The three robes sever the three poisons;
the five-strip lower robe severs attachment to the body.
It is traditionally said that the seven-strip inner robe (antaravāsaka) severs angry speech,
while the great outer robe (saṃghāṭī) severs deluded thoughts.
The seven-strip robe,
the side-fastened jacket,
and the skirt.
It is erroneous to claim that [the Buddha] prescribed only the three robes; the first article of the rules established by Tiantai Zhiyi states:
"The three robes and six articles of requisites must be complete.
If any of these items are lacking..."
Thus, they do not dwell together.
The First of the Ten Vows of National Teacher Qingliang states:
"I shall possess nothing but the three robes and a single alms bowl."
I do not keep any surplus provisions.
Having examined the sutras and śāstras throughout,
and having perused the monastic histories in their entirety.
Thus one comes to know that the sages and worthies have followed in each other's footsteps,
and that China and India share the same spirit;
yet nowadays, people compete one-sidedly for their respective schools of learning.
Do not insist on making distinctions between ourselves and others.
Furthermore, since there is no difference in the manner of shaving the hair,
why should we laboriously divide our schools based on the dyeing of robes?
Those of high standing and profound learning bear witness to this;
let them examine it in detail,
all the more so given the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
These both extensively clarify the merits of the *kāṣāya*.
May the sons of the Buddha who believe in the teachings rely upon them and practice accordingly. 2. Explanation of Names: There are two parts to the explanation of names.
Regarding the initial general name:
it encompasses both the Sūtras and the Vinaya;
alternatively, it is called *kāṣāya*, named after the dyeing of the cloth.
It is called the "robe of the Way," or the "transcendent robe," or the "Dharma robe," or the "robe free from dust."
It is called "the garment of emaciation" because it diminishes the afflictions;
it is called "the lotus garment" because it is free from defiled attachment;
it is called "the garment of intermediate colors" because it is composed of the three primary colors.
It is called the robe of compassion,
the robe of the field of merit, or the bedding.
It is also said that "requisites" (敷具) all refer to bedding and coverlets alike.
As for the specific names:
first, *saṃghāṭī* (梵云僧伽梨).
This is called the *saṃkakṣikā* (undergarment) because it consists of many small strips of cloth;
in terms of its function, it is named the "garment for entering royal palaces, villages, begging for food, and preaching the Dharma," which is worn from time to time.
Second is the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe).
The "medium-priced robe" refers to a garment whose value falls between those of two [other] robes;
it is so named according to its function, being worn by members of the Saṃgha during rituals, recitations, and lectures on the precepts.
The third is the *antarvāsa*, known as the "lower robe," because it occupies the lowest position or is worn at the lower part of the body.

If used for its name, it refers to the various practices such as walking in the monastery grounds, making robes, or entering a village in accordance with the assembly; in these cases, one must not wear it.
If defined by its characteristics, it refers specifically to the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*).
Seven strips,
nine strips,
and even up to twenty-five strips, etc.
The meanings are numerous and varied; here I shall briefly cite one or two.
Third, explaining the seeking of wealth: this section on seeking wealth is divided into two parts.
First, explaining the practice of begging while remaining free from faults.
Therefore, the substance of this Dharma robe must be pure;
such was the practice of the eminent monks of the Western Land of Brahma.
I have often discarded robes made of refuse;
now I wish to act in accordance with the Dharma,
merely remaining free from improper seeking.
The *Shishi Yaoyao Chao* states:
"Gaining [items] through seeking profit or trade does not constitute [a valid acquisition]. The Vinaya says:

"One must not obtain [them] by wrong livelihood," which the sub-commentary (*shu*) explains as follows: "If one obtains [an item] by inciting [others], or by manifesting signs of it so that others may give out of pity, or by feigning a lack [of resources], one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (捨墮) regarding robes and other garments. The sub-commentary further states: "In all such cases, one is not permitted to perform [the ritual] actions [with them]."
Regarding "wrong livelihood" (mithyājīva):
the words are concise while the meaning they contain is vast; to speak of it broadly:
However, with a perverted mind,
they have engaged in greedy defilement and sold the Dharma for profit.
He prostrated before the Buddha,
recited the sutras,
and observed a fast.
Whatever wealth is acquired through various types of karma is all termed "wrong livelihood. Nowadays,
people accumulate vast surpluses in their bags and stores.
They forcibly beg from others;
they employ artful speech and sycophancy;
and their gifts and offerings defile the household.
All such categories as these are collectively termed "evil profits.
Next, the faults of bartering are explained:
it is most excellent if one acquires goods through trade using fundamentally pure wealth.
If one necessarily commits an offense involving money or valuables for the purpose of trading for clothing,
according to the Vinaya, one must forfeit the offending garment;
having forfeited it, one may trade for a new garment.
One should merely repent for previous transgressions;
since the substance of the robe remains unstained,
this principle may be applied by analogy.
If one trades goods oneself, one must not compete with laypeople over high or low prices; this is the law of the marketplace.
If one sends a *kappiyakāraka* (a pure person), [the same applies].
Nor is there any loss incurred.
Some say that pure wealth may be touched with the hands.
This would then constitute impurity;
this is not what is prescribed by the Vinaya.
It is merely a false tradition among people; one only commits the offense of grasping precious objects, but it does not defile the substance of the wealth itself.
4. Clarifying the Substance of Wealth. This section on clarifying the substance of wealth is divided into two parts.
First, clarifying what is in accordance with the Dharma:
within the Vinaya, both silk and cotton cloth are still permitted as materials.
If one follows various passages in the *Yèshù* (Commentary on Karma), silk (*jiàn*) is likewise not permitted.
The *Shù* states: "In the world, silk and raw silk (*zhòu*) are commonly used."
Since its substance involves taking life,
it is likewise subject to prohibition and restraint;
this applies even today among the people of the Five Indias as well as the various foreign monks.
It is said that those who lack both [the means] should make their *kāṣāya* from silk;
furthermore, it is stated that one takes this garment as the "Brahmanic robe."
While practicing the four immeasurables,
one clearly recognizes that [the food] involves killing,
yet intentionally consumes it.
This interpretation is incorrect.
In the *Gantong zhuan*,
a celestial being offered this praise:
Since the transmission of the Buddha-dharma to the East,
for six or seven hundred years,
there have been Vinaya masters of the Northern and Southern schools.
I have never had such an intention;
why should I use wealth acquired through the killing of living beings to make garments for compassion?
This is explained in detail in the *Zhangfuyi* (Ritual for Robes and Ornaments).
Yijing, in his *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*,
arbitrarily censured this practice as being improper.
Indeed, the profound practice of great compassion is not something they can know;
it is truly as it should be.
Next, to exclude what is not the Dharma:
as for the substance of the robe,
it must be sought out to be thick and dense.
One must avoid all that is flowery and ornate.
The Vinaya states:
"If the material is fine, thin, coarse, or made of plantain, hemp, or ramie, it is not permitted; likewise, brocade, silk, and damask are all forbidden."
Silks, fine gauzes, and brocades are all improper items.
Nowadays, many do not believe the Buddha’s words.
Regarding the wearing of these various robes,
the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
"The Tathāgata wore a coarse cotton *saṃghāṭī*."
In this region, the community on Mount Heng and the eminent monks of antiquity who possessed the Way wore robes of coarse hemp and stuffed with mugwort.
Not mixed with even a single thread;
Tiantai wore only a single hempen robe,
while Nanshan used neither silk nor cotton together.
Jingxi wore coarse cloth for his robes;
Yongjia did not consume silk with his mouth.
Was this not because their compassion was profound?
Truly worthy of admiration!
In these times, people are not only negligent,
but moreover lack understanding.
On the contrary, you take the robes prescribed by the Tathāgata for his own regulations and use them as mourning garments;
furthermore, the monastic community has no system of mourning attire.
How can one act so recklessly?
[Refer to] the *Shishi Yaolan* (Essentials for the Śākya Clan) and the *Fujiao Xiaolun* (Treatise on Filial Piety as an Aid to the Teachings).
These are successive corruptions of the teachings;
be careful not to rely upon them.
Recently, I have seen those who use white cloth for their head-bands of mourning.
This is also truly strange.
The signs of the extinction of the Dharma become increasingly frequent with each passing generation.
Those with discernment should reform this;
thus the Dharma may remain for a little longer.
5. Clarifying the Characteristics of Color and Form:
Regarding the Vinaya, it states that one must not wear robes dyed with superior colors.
When one destroys [the original color] to produce the color of a *kāṣāya*—here translated as "improper color" (*asamyak-varṇa*)—it is also called "altered color" (*vikṛta-varṇa*).
This refers to the three types of dyeing for altering color mentioned in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, all of which are in accordance with the Dharma.
The first is blue (*nīla*), according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
This refers to copper-green (t'ung-ch'ing).
Nowadays, the blue-brown robes of the bhikṣuṇī community are quite similar to this.
The second is black, referring to those dyed with dark clay.
Nowadays, the robes of the meditation community are deep black, as well as deep gray and dark brown;
all are identical to black.
The third is the mulan color, which refers to the mulan tree of Western Shu;
its bark can be dyed a reddish-black, and monks of the ancient Jin dynasty often wore robes of this hue.
At present, the light yellow dyed silk from the coastal regions has some degree of overlap [with other shades],
while that from the northern lands is a pale yellow.
This is certainly contrary to the Dharma.
However, these three colors share the same name while differing in substance;
one must distinguish them from the five primary colors of the mundane world—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, and black.
Furthermore, there are five intermediate colors— namely, vermilion, red, purple, green, and azure—
or as some say, crimson and yellow.
None of these are appropriate for the appearance of a practitioner on the Path.
The Buddha prohibited both [types of clothing].
The *Yeshu* states:
"Dharma robes accord with the Way."
The patterns of the brocade are like shimmering silks,
dazzling the mind and spirit;
there are five colors, blue and yellow.
True purple is of the highest quality;
because it is what the common world covets,
it is therefore pared down and reduced.
In this degenerate age,
those who study the Vinaya have specifically contravened the words of the Sage by wearing silk and damask in winter.
In summer, they used fine silk and gauze;
their vermilion hues were disarrayed,
yet they never grew weary of such fresh brilliance.
The dimensions of these illegal [robes] have their hems hanging down past the knees;
how much more so when they themselves delight in colored garments and falsely claim them to be the royal decree.
Although it may be said that this is merely an attempt to gloss over one's faults, it fundamentally constitutes a slander against the Dharma.

This is what the Patriarchs meant when they lamented, "Who would dare not fear the prospect of the evil realms? Alas! To violate the royal edicts as described in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and yet claim to attain auspicious results is a great pity.
This refers merely to violating the prohibitions of the state.
6. Clarifying the Dimensions of the Robe (Cīvara): There are two [parts] to clarifying the dimensions of the robe.
The first follows the general text.
The dimensions are not fixed.
The Vinaya states:
"Measure the body and then make the robe."
One should take only as much as needed.
The measurement of five cubits (*pañca-hasta*) is not fixed;
the Buddha commanded that it be according to the proportions of one's own body.
It is not necessary to rely on the cubit (hasta);
nowadays, robes are one zhang two or three chi in length.
To say that "taking" refers to the literal text—
is this not too broad? Furthermore,
to say that "this is for crossing over the body"— what does this mean?
His body is very small, yet his robe is very long; would it not be too large for him?
Is it not excessive?
However, many people do not understand the method for measuring the body.
The *Yeshu* (Commentary on Karma) states:
"First, using clothing and wealth..."
From the shoulder down to the ground,
and four finger-widths above the ankle,
[the measurement] constitutes the body of the robe.
The remaining characteristics of the leaves are sufficiently proportionate.
Next, the specific measurements are explained.
The Commentary, having already cited the scriptural passage from the *Samyuktāgama*, continues by saying:
"Even so, one must still establish a standard for comparison;
therefore, [the rules of] the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*..."
Each has three grades of measurement.
Now, according to the *Sarvāstivāda* tradition regarding the three robes,
they are five cubits in length.
The width is three cubits, with each cubit being one chi and eight cun;
according to the Zhou standard of King Ji, this measures nine chi in length and five chi four cun in width. As for the largest size:
It is six cubits long and three and a half cubits wide;
it is one zhang eight cun long and six chi three cun wide.
Some people hold a restrictive view regarding its maximum dimensions.
Since it has already been divided into three grades,
how can it be restricted to only one?
Even if we were to rely on this [text],...
Nor should it reach one zhang two chi; if one considers it to be extremely small,
it should be four cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width— that is, seven feet two inches in length and four feet five inches in width— if it exceeds these measurements, it is improper.
If one speaks of it as pure while harboring such thoughts, one commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
The antarvāsa is four cubits in length and two cubits in width;
its length is seven chi and two cun.
The *uttarāsaṅga* is three cubits wide and five cubits long;
it is three cubits wide [at the shoulders].
The *saṃghāṭī* is likewise nine feet in length and five feet four inches in width;
the former citation of the Buddha’s words demonstrates its measurement,
while the latter citation of the Patriarchs’ teachings reveals its incorrectness.
The *Zhangfu yi* (Protocol for Robes and Garments) states:
"They are made in reduced proportions,
conforming to the standard of frugality."
If one exceeds the limit and falsely increases [the count],
there is a rule for committing an offense.
The text says:
Four cubits or two cubits;
it shall not be made in an improper manner,
but equal in measure to that of the Buddha.
This is precisely the proof for the compilation of the *Zhengbian* (Correct Chapters).
Furthermore, it says:
Recently, those at the lower reaches have been arrogant and extravagant in their conduct;
as for those who advocate frugality and restraint,
we have yet to see such a person.
It is further stated:

"Regarding the establishment of measurements for clothing that reduce what is permitted and exceed what is prohibited, these all serve to suppress feelings of greed and competition. Those who desire greatness should examine these various texts in detail."
The *Chao* (Commentary) states regarding the precept on the Buddha’s robes:
"The Buddha’s body is twice that of a human;
the Buddha is sixteen feet tall."
A human being is eight chi tall;
the Buddha’s robe is longer—
according to the scale of the Zhou dynasty of the Ji clan, it is eighteen chi in length and twelve chi in width.
Ordinary people are nine or six chi tall, yet there are those who maintain an extreme measurement, claiming that a Buddha’s robe is twice the human length—namely, two zhang, one chi, and six cun.
This is likely because they have not read this text; for during the Buddha’s lifetime, [the measurements were as follows].
The body is exceedingly magnificent;
its proportions are as previously described,
and his feet cover his entire form.
In the present age of kalpa-decrease,
the human body reaches a maximum height of no more than six chi.
The robes were one zhang and two chi in length,
often exceeding that measure;
as for their width, it was discussed as follows.
If it does not reach five chi in front and trails down to the knees,
there is a *duṣkṛta* offense for every step;
this may truly be called being "upside down."
This is evident therein. Thus, the *Yeshu* (Commentary on the Ritual) states:
"The front [corner] hangs down at a single angle."
It takes on the appearance of an elephant's trunk;
people do not contemplate their transgressions,
and through long habituation, they regard it as the Dharma.
Why must there be such afflictions and self-grasping?
Having been habitually practiced since beginningless time,
can this truly be the Noble Dharma?
"To hear of righteousness and immediately reform it;
to follow counsel as water flows—such is the superior man. Since the text of the *Shuowen* contains such compassionate instruction, how can one fail to contemplate it?
7. Clarifying the Number of Strips. Regarding the number of strips below: the lower robe has five strips, one long and one short.
The inner robe (antarvāsaka) consists of seven strips, with two long and one short.
The outer robe (saṃghāṭī) has three grades;
of these, the lower grade has three [sub-varieties].
The nine-striped, eleven-striped, and thirteen-striped [robes] all consist of two long strips and one short strip;
these are the three middle grades.
The fifteen-, seventeen-, and nineteen-thread [robes] all have three long strips and one short strip.
The three types of superior quality [robes] have twenty-one, twenty-three, and twenty-five threads.
"Four are long and one is short.
The *Chao* states:
"Based on this as the primary standard, one should determine [the dimensions] according to one's capacity among the nine grades."
According to the quantity of the substance of the offering, one receives the *karmavācanā* for formal acceptance. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Ritual) states:
"The reason it reaches a maximum of twenty-five [monks] is as follows:"
Because he wishes to serve as a field of merit for the twenty-five states of existence,
he appears alone and not as a pair;
as a śramaṇa, he nurtures others with benevolence, harmonizing with the world through the transformation of the Yang.
Therefore, they do not form an even number.
As for why they are long or short,
it is like the rice fields in the world, which vary according to the high and low levels of the water.
Furthermore, for the benefit of all sentient beings,
it is manifested that the holy increase while the ordinary decrease,
analogous to how the long becomes more numerous while the short become fewer.
At present, many in the Chan school wear robes of nine strips;
some make them with three long panels and four short ones according to their own whims.
This is not in accordance with the Dharma.
The Commentary states:
"Because the variations in length and brevity deviate from the *brahman* [of compassion],
one's steps accordingly transgress the ritual protocol."
Each instance constitutes an offense;
moreover, the robes have long trailing ends,
the flowers are arranged with fine thorns, and they are like mountain-water woolen cloaks.
To let one's practice decline and one's efforts go to waste is to fail in the sincere study of the Way, which does not spare even a moment of time;
this can only occur if one has no application of mind.
What leisure do I have to devote my efforts exclusively to this?
Next, I shall clarify the characteristics of the branches and leaves,
as found in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
The width should be four finger-breadths or four cun, with the sides shaped like a grain of barley.
The Commentary states:
"Nowadays, many make them wide; this is a spreading of improper customs."
The *Zhangfu yi* states:
"These observations of minor details are not appended to the formal ritual."
"Three or four inches [of cloth] may be opened wide as one pleases;
this has gradually become a custom,
further opening the source of frivolous extravagance," and so forth.
Furthermore, when sewing on strips and leaves,
one must open the lower edge.
The *Zhangfu yi* states:
When a tailor sees the surface of a leaf, he can discern its cut edges;
now that they have been sewn together, there are no such edges to distinguish.
The *Chao* says:
One side is pierced and the other is opened;
if both sides were sewn together,
it would be no different from a plain robe (*maṇḍala-cīvara*).
It is commonly transmitted in the world that this is called "bright aperture" (*mingkong*).
Furthermore, it is said that "bright appearance" (*mingxiang*) refers to the sky at dawn; others also say it refers to "leakage-dust" (*louchen*) and so forth.
Both [of these views] are erroneous.
8. Explaining the Frequency of Layers: The Vinaya states, "It must not be thin or flimsy."
A new *saṃghāṭī* consists of two layers;
the other two robes are each single-layered.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, an old *saṃghāṭī* consists of four layers.
Regarding the other two robes, both are double-layered; according to the Sarvāstivāda school,
the great robe (saṃghāṭī) is triple-layered because it consists of one new layer and two double-layered layers.
Next, the gravity of the offenses is explained.
However, regarding the characteristics of these repetitions,
various sources differ.
If one follows the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, when the three robes (*tricīvara*) are sewn together with double seams,
they may be temporarily separated and worn for specific reasons;
based on this, it is merely that.
The entire robe is joined together;
what the Patriarch wore was no different from this.
In the *Zhigan Tongzhuan*, Tianren indicated that a separate version should be produced;
many people have doubted this, so I shall now cite it in full.
It states: "The *kaṣāya* (great robe) should be made double-layered."
The Master followed this practice;
however, beneath the leaves,
there were actually three layers.
"How could that be so? he asked, inquiring about what had been done;
he then grasped my robe.
This was shown to him.
These leaf-marks represent the ridges and boundaries of a rice paddy field.
Using pieces of cut-up cloth,
stitch them on the inside,
leaving a space about the size of a leaf or a grain of barley.
This refers to the depiction of the fields within the strips and the depiction of the irrigation channels upon the leaves; is this not so?
Now, however, it is represented by a continuous expanse of cloth.
First, it is not cut;
second, it is also multi-layered.
Since these do not conform to the original regulations, [they are not permitted].
The fault of being non-attached while still attached has already been explained in the preceding text.
As for the fact that the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* differs from this,
it is merely due to a discrepancy in what was heard or seen.
However, the teachings revealed by the devas and humans all claim to have been personally received from the Buddha’s own era; thus,
matters that remain undecided within the scriptural texts of this region [are clarified].
As stated in various sūtras and vinayas,
the sitting mat (niṣīdana) is worn over the shoulder;
this is the only such account found in the transmitted texts.
Place it upon the left arm.
Furthermore, as in the subsequent citation regarding the method for increasing the seat-cloth (*niṣīdana*),
all current practices should follow this standard.
Why doubt only this?
Moreover, it is not merely a matter of resolving the two difficulties regarding the multiple and the double;
the principle is self-evident. As the *Sanming chengbukeye shu* states: [text follows].
The latter two [robes] may be worn according to the occasion;
however, if it is the outer robe (saṃghāṭī),
it must necessarily be double-layered.
Nowadays, many people wear these non-Dharmic robes;
while they may obtain and maintain them,
wearing them constitutes an offense.
9. Clarifying the Method for Making Robes (9): Clarifying the Method for Making Robes. The three robes must all be made from cut-and-sewn patches.
If resources are scarce and it is difficult to procure them, then folding the cloth [into strips] is permitted.
The five strips constitute one kind;
furthermore, they may be folded like leaves.
